source.title: A Diffusion Theory For Deep Learning Dynamics: Stochastic Gradient Descent Exponentially Favors Flat Minima
source.authors: Zeke Xie; Issei Sato; Masashi Sugiyama

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures how SGD escape rates depend on sharpness, batch size, and learning rate, but it does not measure train-to-test error gaps or held-out generalization described by the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports escape-rate experiments and Hessian/noise-covariance measurements. These do not directly measure any claim version's generalization outcome, so their rows are recorded under none.
record.test_reason: The study measures SGD escape dynamics and gradient-noise structure, not held-out performance or generalization gaps. Its proposed explanation of large-batch behavior does not test V5, and its Hessian-based escape measure does not test V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. Under their diffusion assumptions, the authors conclude that SGD selects flat minima with exponentially greater probability than sharp minima. They report escape-time dependence exponential in inverse path sharpness and the batch-size-to-learning-rate ratio, supported by escape simulations; they do not demonstrate corresponding held-out generalization effects.
record.recipe_differences: The empirical measurements concern minima escape dynamics and Hessian/noise covariance, rather than train/test generalization outcomes or the listed original interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Escape-rate relations are examined while varying minima sharpness, batch size, and learning rate; the paper reports that each affects escape rate exponentially.

fits_no_version.finding: Across four tabular datasets, negative log escape rate is approximately linear in inverse sharpness scale, batch size, and inverse learning rate.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the tested pretrained networks, SGD escapes faster with sharper rescaled landscapes, smaller batches, and larger learning rates, following the predicted exponential relations.

fits_no_version.finding: Gradient-noise covariance approximately tracks the Hessian divided by batch size; injected-white-noise experiments show a polynomial rather than exponential sharpness dependence.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hessian-dependent stochastic-gradient noise produces different minima escape and selection dynamics from injected isotropic noise.

record.problems: The escape theory depends on second-order Taylor, quasi-equilibrium, and low-temperature assumptions. The paper says experiments require tuned hyperparameters for pretrained models; figures summarize relations without per-condition numerical escape-rate values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Not included: Styblinski-Tang test-function escape experiments and artificial-data experiments in Appendix E, because the retained rows cover each reported sharpness, batch-size, and learning-rate relation for the real-world neural-network experiments. Also not included: Hessian/noise-covariance correlation and Gaussian-noise histogram measurements, which concern gradient-noise structure rather than the listed generalization versions.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting alongside natural-label generalization and chance-level random-label held-out accuracy. Appendix E uses random labels only for escape experiments.
Held-out error as width increases beyond the width needed to fit training data.
Held-out comparisons of convolutional and fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive-optimizer versus SGD held-out performance under limited or broader tuning. The SGD–Adam flatness comparison is attributed to another paper.
Held-out performance across batch sizes with fixed epoch budgets, longer training, or adapted recipes.
Dropout effects on held-out error across data sizes, dropout strengths, and augmentation regimes.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, its correlation with train–test gaps, and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Test-accuracy effects of removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All retained experiments start from models pretrained for 200–1000 epochs. Escape means leaving a specified parameter neighborhood, with 100 repetitions per setting. Hyperparameters were tuned separately for pretrained models. The cannot_determine states concern the listed claim versions, not whether the escape-rate relations were reported.

versions.untested_parts: Memorization of random labels and held-out performance on natural and random labels.
Test error as network width increases beyond the interpolation threshold.
Test-error comparison of convolutional and fully connected architectures.
Held-out performance comparison of adaptive optimizers and SGD.
Held-out performance comparison across batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Effect of dropout on held-out error.
The paper studies sharpness and escape rates, but does not measure train-to-test gaps or magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness.
Effect of removing memorized examples on test accuracy.

rows.subject: fully-connected network
rows.operation_detail: Measured escape rate as minima sharpness was varied by rescaling the landscape.
rows.measure: Escape rate versus path Hessian sharpness; the paper states that − log(γ) is linear with 1/k.
rows.value: The escape rate exponentially depends on the minima sharpness.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence interval formula for the estimated escape rate is given; per-condition bounds not stated.
rows.note: Reports the escape-rate relation, not a generalization-gap measure.
rows.check: Escape rate under landscape rescaling cannot establish any version's generalization effect; the reported escape relation itself is observed.
